headline: Five forecaster groups outside any single lab now price the coding-rung-to-research-rung interval, and they land between 3.6 and 37 months with a centre near 12; every one of those figures is a forecast, and the two benchmarks that measure research work apart from coding put frontier agents at 23.2% of a human-team reference and RE-Bench at 0.5-0.8 against the 1.3 that early 2026 was supposed to bring.

evidence.claim: Superhuman coder to superhuman AI researcher: aggregate median 0.55 years (6.6 months), range 0 to 2.1 years, from four professional forecasters at FutureSearch (Tom Liptay, Finn Hambly, Sergio Abriola, Tolga Bilge) commissioned as an external check on the AI 2027 takeoff model.
evidence.source: AI 2027 Takeoff Forecast, ai-2027.com/research/takeoff-forecast

evidence.claim: AI 2027 authors' own SC-to-SAR figure: median 0.3 years (3.6 months), with 15% probability the two rungs coincide at 0 years; the underlying human-only crossing time is median 4 years, 80% CI 1.5 to 10 years, lognormal, divided by a 5x AI R&D speedup at SC.
evidence.source: Kokotajlo & Lifland, AI 2027 Takeoff Forecast

evidence.claim: Automated Coder to Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI, all-things-considered median gaps: Kokotajlo 8.9 months (AC Nov 2027, TED-AI Nov 2028), Lifland 1.1 years (AC Jan 2030, TED-AI Jul 2032), Halstead AC Jan 2029 to TED-AI Apr 2031 (27 months by date subtraction). The model's own milestone order runs AC, SAR, SIAR, TED-AI, ASI, so each figure bounds AC-to-SAR from above.
evidence.source: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue, blog.aifutures.org

evidence.claim: Milestone definitions the interval rests on: AC is "an AC can fully automate an AGI project's coding work, replacing the project's entire coding staff"; SAR is "a SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete".
evidence.source: AI Futures Model: Dec 2025 Update, Kokotajlo, Lifland, Halstead, Kastner

evidence.claim: Metaculus community medians for OpenAI reporting AI Self-improvement risk levels: High 09 Jun 2029, Critical Jul 2032, a 37-month spread, from 54 forecasters. Question closes 31 Dec 2040.
evidence.source: Metaculus question 38787, "Dates that OpenAI reports an AI reached these Self-improvement risk levels?", read in browser

evidence.claim: The two rungs that pair of medians spans: High is "the model's impact is equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher a highly performant mid-career research engineer assistant, relative to those researchers' 2024 baseline"; Critical is "the model is capable of recursively self improving (i.e., fully automated AI R&D), defined as either (leading indicator) a superhuman research-scientist agent OR (lagging indicator) causing a generational model improvement... in 1/5th the wall-clock time of equivalent progress in 2024... sustainably for several months". High sits below a superhuman coding rung, so 37 months reads as an upper bound.
evidence.source: OpenAI Preparedness Framework Version 2, p.11 tracked-category table

evidence.claim: Metaculus community medians for Anthropic reporting AI R&D risk levels: Level 4 on 14 Sep 2026, Level 5 on 26 Jul 2028, a 22.4-month spread, from 3 forecasters. AI R&D-4 is the ability to fully automate the work of an entry-level, remote-only Researcher at Anthropic; AI R&D-5 is the ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling, quantified as a one-year scale-up of roughly 1000x.
evidence.source: Metaculus question 38791 read in browser; thresholds from Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy (disaggregation recorded in the v3.1 changelog, RSP v3.0 dated 2026-02-24)

evidence.claim: Metaculus community medians for Google's Machine Learning R&D critical capability levels: autonomy level 1 on 23 Jan 2027, uplift level 1 on 29 Mar 2027, from 6 forecasters. Autonomy level 1 ("can fully automate the AI R&D pipeline at a competitive cost") is the harder rung and is priced 2 months ahead of uplift level 1 ("AI progress substantially accelerating, e.g. 2x, from 2020-2024 rates"), so this panel is too thin to order the rungs.
evidence.source: Metaculus question 38789 read in browser; definitions from Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework v2.0 (2025-02-04) via ETO AGORA

evidence.claim: Differencing two median dates overstates the median gap. Lifland's published AC-to-TED-AI median gap is 1.1 years while his median dates stand 30 months apart, a factor of 2.27; Kokotajlo's is 8.9 months against 12 months of date difference, a factor of 1.35. Mean correction 1.8x, measured on the only two cases where both quantities are published.
evidence.source: AI Futures Project, Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update

evidence.claim: Direct measurement of research-task automation apart from coding: on autonomous LLM post-training under 10 hours on one H100, the best frontier agent reaches 23.2% weighted average benchmark performance against 51.1% for official instruction-tuned models produced by human teams. The paper opens by noting agents "have become surprisingly proficient at software engineering over the past year" and asks whether that extends to research.
evidence.source: Rank, Bhatnagar, Prabhu, Eisenberg, Nguyen, Bethge, Andriushchenko, PostTrainBench, arXiv:2603.08640v2 (ELLIS Institute Tubingen, MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tubingen AI Center)

evidence.claim: RE-Bench, the ML research-engineering suite scored against 71 8-hour attempts by 61 human experts, stands at 0.5 to 0.8 for frontier models against the 1.3 that AI 2027 predicted for early 2026; external forecasters project 1.0 arriving in 2027.
evidence.source: AI 2027 Tracker, RE-Bench prediction page

evidence.claim: Frontier 50% time horizon on software tasks is about 12 hours, and Anthropic explicitly argues it had not seen a 2x increase in the pace of progress as of April 2026. Agents performed below the 20th percentile on threat-modelling work, and the report carries no quantitative measure for automating conceptual research tasks.
evidence.source: METR, Frontier Risk Report (February to March 2026)

evidence.claim: Time horizons across domains cluster: software, math contests and scientific QA all sit at 50 to 200 minute horizons doubling every 2 to 6 months, while agentic computer use runs 40-100x shorter at similar rates, which METR reads as roughly 2 years behind. This supplies the conversion from a measured horizon ratio to a lag in months: months = log2(ratio) x doubling months.
evidence.source: METR, How Does Time Horizon Vary Across Domains?

evidence.claim: The measurement of AI R&D automation is at the proposal stage. A GovAI paper argues existing capability benchmarks "may not reflect real-world automation" and recommends companies and third parties begin tracking capital share of AI R&D spending, researcher time allocation, and AI subversion incidents. Its benchmark discussion names SWE-bench, MLE-bench, RE-Bench and PaperBench and reports no interval between coding and research capability.
evidence.source: Chan, Padarath, Kwon, Greaves, Anderljung, Measuring AI R&D Automation, arXiv:2603.03992

evidence.claim: Conditional on AI exceeding human performance on month-long research projects, the probability of 3x effective-compute acceleration by 2029 is 20.5% among 8 AI forecasting domain experts and 18% among 10 superforecasters. Unconditionally the same groups give 20% and 8%.
evidence.source: METR, Forecasting the Impacts of AI R&D Acceleration: Results of a Pilot Study

evidence.claim: Prediction markets do not price this interval. A Manifold API search for "superhuman coder", "automate AI research" and "superhuman AI researcher" returns no market on the gap; the nearest, "Will AI research be automated within the next 2 years?", carries 905 mana of volume. Metaculus carries no question on the AI 2027 SC-to-SAR interval itself; its three lab-threshold questions above are the closest instruments and hold 54, 6 and 3 forecasters.
evidence.source: api.manifold.markets/v0/search-markets; metaculus.com question feed searches for "AI R&D automation" and "automate AI research"

evidence.claim: The largest expert survey cannot supply this interval by differencing its own questions. In the 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers, the median for high-level machine intelligence is 2047 and for full automation of labour 2116, a roughly 70-year gap the authors themselves flag as a framing effect between task-framed and occupation-framed questions rather than a real interval.
evidence.source: Grace et al., Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI, arXiv:2401.02843, survey fielded October 2023

evidence.claim: The 2026 consensus report backed by 30+ countries and over 100 experts records "little expert consensus" on whether progress plateaus, continues, or accelerates through AI systems speeding up AI research.
evidence.source: International AI Safety Report 2026, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, arXiv:2602.21012

recommendedNumber:
Axis K prior: 15% point mass at 0 months (the rungs coincide), and 85% lognormal with median 12 months and an 80% CI of 4 to 38 months.

The arithmetic. Seven forecaster-group estimates of the coding-rung-to-research-rung interval, in months:
  3.6  AI 2027 authors, SC to SAR, 2025-04
  6.6  FutureSearch n=4, SC to SAR, 2025-04
  8.9  Kokotajlo, AC to TED-AI, 2026-08-16
 13.2  Lifland, AC to TED-AI, 2026-08-16
 22.4  Metaculus n=3, Anthropic AI R&D-4 to R&D-5, 2026-08-17
 27.0  Halstead, AC to TED-AI, 2026-08-16
 37.0  Metaculus n=54, OpenAI self-improvement High to Critical, 2026-08-17
Median 13.2. Geometric mean exp((1.281+1.887+2.186+2.580+3.109+3.296+3.611)/7) = exp(2.564) = 13.0 months.

Three of those seven (22.4, 27.0, 37.0) are differences of median dates rather than medians of a gap. The AI Futures update publishes both quantities in two cases and the difference-of-medians runs 1.35x and 2.27x high, mean 1.8x. Dividing those three by 1.8 gives 12.4, 15.0, 20.6, and the corrected set is 3.6, 6.6, 8.9, 12.4, 13.2, 15.0, 20.6: median 12.4, geometric mean 10.1. Round the centre to 12 months.

Width from the raw spread: sigma_ln = ln(37.0/3.6) / (2 x 1.2816) = 2.330 / 2.563 = 0.909. Then 12 x exp(+/- 1.2816 x 0.909) = 12 x [0.312, 3.21] = 3.7 to 38.5 months, rounded to 4 to 38.

The 15% at zero is carried from the one source that quantifies coincidence: AI 2027 assigns 15% to SC already being SAR, and FutureSearch's range runs down to 0.

Two directions to hold the band open rather than tighten it. Every one of the seven is a forecast, and five of the seven come from people who read each other; the two Metaculus panels that are structurally independent of the AI Futures circle sit at the high end (22.4 and 37 months raw). Against that, the three cheapest-to-check figures are the two oldest: the FutureSearch 6.6 and the AI 2027 3.6 date from April 2025 and have not been re-run, while both authors' coding-rung medians have since moved by years in both directions.

If the published axis currently carries a band narrower than a factor of 5, widen it: the ratio between the highest and lowest independent estimate is 37.0/3.6 = 10.3.
whatWouldSettleIt:
One measurement, published on a single axis, closes this: separate time-horizon curves for research tasks and for coding tasks drawn from the same task suite and calibrated in human-expert hours, so the horizontal offset between the two curves reads directly in months. METR already holds the pieces on both sides — RE-Bench research-engineering environments with 71 8-hour human-expert attempts, and HCAST plus the shorter software tasks — and already reports the doubling rate needed for the conversion (2 to 6 months across intellectual domains, 14 Jul 2025). What is missing is the split: the published curve pools "software and research tasks" into one series, and the 12-hour 50% horizon of 19 May 2026 is that pooled figure. With a split, a measured horizon ratio r between the two families converts by months = log2(r) x doubling months, giving the K interval as a measured quantity with an error bar rather than as a panel median.

Two supporting series would let it be checked while the coding rung is still uncrossed. First, the GovAI metrics of 4 Mar 2026 reported quarterly by the labs — capital share of AI R&D spending and researcher time allocation — which would show the coding rung being crossed inside a company before any public benchmark records it. Second, a repeat of PostTrainBench's 23.2%-against-51.1% comparison at a fixed cadence: the date that ratio reaches 1.0 is the research rung arriving, and the date a coding benchmark of matched human-hours reaches 1.0 is the coding rung, and the difference is K measured once rather than forecast seven times.

Until either exists, the honest statement is that the interval has been priced and never measured, and that the earliest it becomes measurable is the moment the first rung is crossed.

headline: Two of the six domains now carry fitted rates that differ from software by 1.4x and 3.7x (cyber 4.7-9.8 months, self-driving 20 months against software's 4-7 months), two more (forecasting, persuasion) are measured at or above human-expert level in 2026 while the model dates them to 2029 and 2031, and biosciences and novel science hold zero length-calibrated trend of any kind.

evidence.claim: Software reference rate: the 50% time horizon doubles every 196 days across 2019-2026, every 131 days for models released after 2023, and every 89 days for models released from 2024 onward, from one dataset of 228 tasks (31 of them 8+ hours, 5 of those with measured human baselines).
evidence.source: METR, Time Horizon 1.1

evidence.claim: Cross-domain spread as first measured: Tesla FSD doubles near 20 months (0.6 doublings per year) against 2-6 months for the software and reasoning cluster (SWE-bench Verified, GPQA Diamond, LiveCodeBench, MATH), Mock AIME near 3 months, and visual computer use (OSWorld, WebArena) at 40-100x shorter horizons rising at similar rates. RLBench (robotics) carries overall scores with no fitted doubling; the authors call it a weak benchmark with task durations estimated from demonstration lengths.
evidence.source: METR, How Does Time Horizon Vary Across Domains?

evidence.claim: Cyber, instrument one: the 80%-reliability cyber time horizon doubles every 4.7 months since late 2024, measured February 2026, against 8 months at both 50% and 80% measured November 2025. The same post puts METR's software figure at 4.2 months over the same window. Over a third of tasks are timed with human experts, the rest estimated, at a 2.5M token limit.
evidence.source: UK AI Security Institute, How fast is autonomous AI cyber capability advancing?

evidence.claim: Cyber, instrument two: 9.8 months for 2019+ (95% CI 4.8-11.2, R2 = 0.95) and 5.7 months for 2024+, by item response theory over 291 tasks across seven benchmarks (CyBashBench, NL2Bash, InterCode-CTF, NYUCTF, CyBench, CVEBench, CyberGym), models through Opus 4.6. Frontier models sit at 3.1-3.2 hours of expert time at 50% success. The authors call these lower bounds at a 2M token budget.
evidence.source: Lyptus Research, Offensive Cybersecurity Time Horizons

evidence.claim: Forecasting, instrument one: superforecasters lead the best LLMs by 0.017 Brier points; LLM scores improve about 0.015 Brier points per year (Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.117 to Grok 4.20 0.102); parity extrapolated to November 2026, 95% CI January 2026 to November 2027, with dataset questions at June 2026 and market questions at August 2026.
evidence.source: Forecasting Research Institute, ForecastBench

evidence.claim: Forecasting, instrument two: professional forecasters beat bots head to head every quarter, spot peer score -11.3 (Q3 2024), -8.9 (Q4 2024), -17.7 (Q1 2025), -20.0 (Q2 2025, 95% CI -28.6 to -11.4, p = 0.00001, 93 overlapping questions). The authors state they cannot discern any trend in whether bots are closing, because the quarterly intervals overlap. Ten Pros place above the top bot.
evidence.source: Metaculus quarterly AI benchmark results

evidence.claim: Biosciences, level rather than rate: across 27 models, GPQA-Bio rose 42% to 81%, CloningScenarios 23% to 61%, ProtocolQA 31% to 72% between late 2022 and early 2025; o3 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking were the first above the PhD baseline on CloningScenarios; o3 reached 46.1% on VCT-Text against an expert virologist baseline of 22.6%. These are accuracy series on fixed sets with no human-time labels, so no horizon can be fitted from them.
evidence.source: Justen et al., LLMs outperform experts on multiple biology benchmarks, arXiv 2505.06108

evidence.claim: Biosciences, the only official trend statement: chemistry and biology performance relative to a PhD baseline moved from -0.4 in 2022 to +0.6 in 2025, about 0.33 baseline units per year, with no doubling time given for the domain.
evidence.source: UK AI Security Institute, Frontier AI Trends Report

evidence.claim: Persuasion, scale: 720 messages from 24 models across several orders of magnitude of size, tested on 25,982 participants, show sharply diminishing returns; the association between size and persuasiveness shrinks toward zero and loses significance once mere task completion is adjusted for, and frontier models are already at ceiling on task completion.
evidence.source: Hackenburg et al., PNAS 122(10)

evidence.claim: Persuasion, levers: across 19 models, 707 issues and 76,977 participants, post-training raised persuasiveness by up to 51% and prompting by up to 27%, both above model scale and personalization; the same methods lowered factual accuracy.
evidence.source: Hackenburg et al., Science

evidence.claim: Persuasion, by generation: within one study (August 2025, N = 12,988) Claude Sonnet 4 scored 0.224 on immigration, Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.209, GPT-4.1 0.190, Grok 4 0.188; within the second (November 2025, N = 6,157) Claude Sonnet 4.5 0.187, GPT-5 0.156, Gemini 3 0.147, Grok 4 0.118. All exceeded human campaign advertisements at 0.135. Release order and general capability rank fail to predict the persuasion order.
evidence.source: Benchmarking Political Persuasion Risks Across Frontier LLMs, arXiv 2603.09884

evidence.claim: Persuasion, level against expert humans: four preregistered experiments, 18,978 conversations from 6,923 people, find frontier systems out-persuade world-champion debaters and professional canvassers who chose their own topics, prepared, and competed for GBP 1,000 prizes, and raise close to 3x the real-money donations professional canvassers raise. Information density per conversation is the mechanism.
evidence.source: Hackenburg et al. (AI Security Institute and Oxford), AI systems out-persuade expert humans, arXiv 2606.16475

evidence.claim: Robotics: a full 2026 survey of industrial, household and navigation tasks reports high-precision insertion at 52% average reliability (Physical Intelligence Olympics), warehouse picking above 99% at 4x slower than humans, DYNA-1 folding 850+ napkins over 24 hours at 99.4% success and 60% of human speed, and declines to fit any time trend, on the ground that a task solved in demonstration is brittle in deployment.
evidence.source: Epoch AI, Where Autonomy Works: Evaluating Robot Capabilities in 2026

evidence.claim: Novel science, the one instrument with two dated points: FrontierMath Tier 4 holds 43 problems each requiring multiple hours to multiple days of a specialist. GPT-5.5 Pro scored 39.6% in April 2026; GPT-5.6 Sol scored 83.0% on 2026-08-07. The v2 revision of 2026-06-12 sits between the two points, having corrected 135 problems and removed 12.
evidence.source: Epoch AI, FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2)

evidence.claim: Novel science, discrete series: a DeepMind agent autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdos problems at a few hundred dollars each (May 2026); OpenAI announced a proof on the unit distance problem on 2026-05-20 and three further Erdos solutions on 2026-08-01; Bloom's database stood at 565 solved and 652 open on 2026-08-03. Counts of resolved problems carry no task-length calibration, so no doubling time follows from them.
evidence.source: Quanta Magazine, Why the Legendary Erdos Problems Are Falling to AI

evidence.claim: The aggregate index used as a cross-domain scalar reports no per-domain rates: frontier improvement runs at 8.337 ECI points per year before 2024-04-08 and 15.459 after.
evidence.source: Epoch AI, AI capabilities progress has sped up

recommendedNumber:
Replace the single tempo scalar with a per-domain rate multiplier r (rate relative to the software and reasoning cluster), applied as an effective threshold on the shared curve: c*_k = 2.6 + (th_k - 2.6) / r_k.

The multipliers, with their arithmetic.
CODE r = 1.00, reference. METR 196 days all-time, 89 days for 2024+ models (2026-01-29).
HACK r = 0.69, band 0.51-0.89. Three same-window pairs: AISI cyber 4.7 mo against METR software 4.2 mo = 0.89; Lyptus 2019+ 9.8 mo against METR 196 days (6.44 mo) = 0.66; Lyptus 2024+ 5.7 mo against METR 89 days (2.92 mo) = 0.51. Mean 0.69. The 0.89 pair mixes an 80% bar with a 50% bar.
R&D r = 1.00. METR's own suite is research engineering, so this domain defines the reference.
ROBOT r = 0.27, band 0.20-0.35. Tesla FSD 20 months against software's 4 months = 0.20 and against 7 months = 0.35; geometric mean 0.27. This is a self-driving proxy standing in for embodiment, because Epoch declines to fit robotics and METR calls RLBench weak.
FCAST, POLIT, BIO, SCI carry no fitted rate. Two of them carry a measured level instead, which is the stronger anchor.

Date effect, computed on the T2 knots (2.6 at 2026.6, 3.0 at 2029.0, 4.0 at 2030.5, 5.0 at 2032.5, 6.0 at 2034.5).
HACK th 3.1: c* = 2.6 + 0.5/0.69 = 3.32, moving 2029.2 to 2029.5, +4 months (band +1 to +8 months).
ROBOT th 4.5: c* = 2.6 + 1.9/0.27 = 9.64, moving 2031.5 to 2041.8, +10.3 years (band +7.1 to +15.2). Under T1 the same multiplier gives +4.1 years, under T3 +22.9.
FCAST th 3.3: ForecastBench dates parity at 2026.9 (CI 2026.0-2027.9) against the curve's 2029.5, a pull of -2.6 years; the Metaculus head-to-head series leaves it where it is. Hold the band 2026.9 to 2029.5.
POLIT th 4.3: the measured bar (out-persuading expert debaters and canvassers) was crossed by 2026.5 against the curve's 2031.1, a pull of -4.6 years, and the scale elasticity is near zero, so this rung should sit early and flat rather than at 4.3.
BIO th 4.1: no rate exists. Its binding step is the wet-lab cycle, which is embodiment-clocked, so the defensible structural change is to give BIO the ROBOT multiplier on its experimental half, which lands it after ROBOT rather than 11 years ahead of it.
SCI th 4.6: no rate exists outside mathematics, where FrontierMath Tier 4 moved 39.6% (April 2026) to 83.0% (2026-08-07) on hours-to-days specialist problems, faster than the curve implies for 2031.7.

The single headline number. One scalar spreads the eight rungs over 2.7 years under T2 (1.1 under T1, 5.4 under T3). The measured evidence spreads them from 2026.5 (persuasion) to 2041.8 (robotics), 15.3 years under T2, 5.9 under T1, 32.9 under T3. Ratios 5.4x, 5.7x, 6.1x. So: widen the inter-domain spread by 5.5x, band 5.4-6.1, implemented as r = {CODE 1.00, HACK 0.69, R&D 1.00, ROBOT 0.27} plus measured-date anchors for FCAST (2026.9) and POLIT (2026.5), and BIO and SCI flagged as uninstrumented.
whatWouldSettleIt: A length-calibrated suite per domain, with human expert timings and repeated dated runs, is what turns four of these into fitted rates. Concretely: (1) biosciences — attach expert-hours labels to LABBench2's ~1,900 tasks and re-run against eight or more dated frontier checkpoints, which converts an accuracy series into a horizon and yields the first bio doubling time with a CI; (2) robotics — publish mean time between interventions on real hardware for dated policy releases (the AutoInspect industrial deployment reports 78 hours, a single point), so embodiment stops being dated by a Tesla proxy METR itself calls biased by selective use conditions; (3) novel science — label a research-frontier suite in specialist-days (FrontierMath Tier 4 already is, at 43 problems) and re-run it quarterly on a frozen version, so the 39.6% to 83.0% move can be separated from the 2026-06-12 problem revision; (4) forecasting — measure horizon as resolution lag (how far ahead a system beats the crowd) rather than Brier at fixed lag, which is what reconciles ForecastBench's November 2026 parity date with the Metaculus head-to-head null. Until (1) and (3) exist, biosciences at 4.1 and novel science at 4.6 are dated by assumption alone, and any per-domain vector should carry them as unmeasured rather than as 1.0.

headline: Across 21 nuclear, chemical, biological and export-control instruments coded 1949–2026, agreements between adversaries lapse at 2.5% per year when bilateral, 0.8% per year when multilateral with a verification organ, and 0.4% per year when informal with no verification at all — and all four bilateral agreements that were violated ended, median 4.1 years after the finding.

evidence.claim: Lippert codes 40 conventional arms control agreements covering Europe since the end of the First World War and finds 8 extreme violation cases, of which 7 contributed to an outbreak of war; the Soviet Union and Russia are implicated in over half the extreme cases. 8/40 = 20% of agreements suffer a severe violation.
evidence.source: William E. Lippert, 'Infrequent but serious: severe conventional arms control agreement violations', Defense & Security Analysis, DOI 10.1080/14751798.2025.2539630 (abstract retrieved via Semantic Scholar)

evidence.claim: A companion Lippert study of 22 conventional agreements from 1918 to 2017 scores 13 fully successful, 5 partially successful, 4 unsuccessful. Outcomes sit on a 0.0–1.0 continuum; the study does not separate lapse from violation as categories.
evidence.source: William Lippert, 'Conventional Arms Control Agreements in Europe: Conditions of Success and Failure', CEJISS

evidence.claim: INF: signed 1987-12-08, in force 1988-06-01, terminated 2019-08-02 — 31.2 years. 2,692 missiles eliminated by the 1991-06-01 deadline (846 US, 1,846 Soviet). The on-site inspection regime ran to 2001-05-31, 13.0 years of a 31.2-year treaty; the remaining 18.2 years ran on national technical means. The SSC-8 (9M729) was tested from 2008; the US withdrawal notice was 2019-02-01.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty; Arms Control Association, US-Soviet/Russian nuclear arms control agreements at a glance

evidence.claim: ABM: signed 1972-05-26, in force 1972-10-03, US withdrawal announced 2001-12-13 and effective 2002-06-13 — 29.7 years. Verification was national technical means alone, plus the first treaty ban on interfering with the other side's NTM. Soviet Foreign Minister Shevardnadze conceded on 1989-10-23 that the Krasnoyarsk radar violated the treaty, six years after the US first raised it.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, ABM Treaty at a Glance; Asia Times, 'How to deal with arms control treaty violations: the Krasnoyarsk radar story'

evidence.claim: New START: signed 2010-04-08, in force 2011-02-05, extended once on 2021-02-03, expired 2026-02-05 — 15.0 years. On-site inspections stopped in March 2020 and never resumed, so verification functioned for 9.1 of 15.0 years, 61% of the treaty's life.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, 'Russia Suspends New START'; Arms Control Association, US-Soviet/Russian agreements at a glance

evidence.claim: The US State Department determined on 2023-01-31 that Russia had failed to comply with New START by refusing inspections and refusing to convene the Bilateral Consultative Commission; Putin announced suspension of participation on 2023-02-21. Time from finding to treaty expiry: 3.0 years.
evidence.source: US Department of State, 2023 Report to Congress on Implementation of the New START Treaty; Arms Control Association

evidence.claim: New START expired on 2026-02-05 with no successor and no negotiations planned. Russia offered in September 2025 to observe the central quantitative limits informally for one year without verification; the US did not respond before expiry. For the first time in more than fifty years there are no binding limits on US and Russian strategic arsenals.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, 'New START Expires As U.S. Urges Modernized Treaty'

evidence.claim: Agreed Framework (US–DPRK): signed 1994-10-21, collapsed after the US announced on 2002-10-16 that the DPRK had acknowledged a uranium enrichment programme; the DPRK removed IAEA seals and cameras at Yongbyon on 2002-12-21. Held 8.2 years. Verification was IAEA seals and monitoring at one site.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, 'North Korea Admits Secret Nuclear Weapons Program'; IAEA Fact Sheet on DPRK Nuclear Safeguards

evidence.claim: CFE: signed 1990-11-19, in force 1992-11-09, Russia suspended 2007-12-12, Russia withdrew 2023-11-07, NATO suspension effective 2023-12-07 — 31.1 years. Verification produced more than 4,000 on-site inspections and more than 52,000 pieces of treaty-limited equipment destroyed between 1992 and 2008.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, CFE Treaty and Adapted CFE Treaty at a Glance

evidence.claim: Open Skies: signed 1992-03-24, in force 2002-01-01, US withdrawal notice 2020-05-22 effective 2020-11-22, Russia's formal withdrawal signed 2021-06-07. More than 1,500 observation flights took place between 2002 and 2019. The treaty was itself the verification instrument.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Treaty on Open Skies; Arms Control Association, Open Skies Treaty at a Glance

evidence.claim: The IAEA Board of Governors has found a state in non-compliance with its NPT safeguards agreement on five occasions to 2006: Iraq 1991, Romania 1992, North Korea 1993, Libya 2004, Iran 2006. Syria followed in 2011 and Iran again on 2025-06-12 (GOV/2025/38). Seven findings across roughly 190 parties in 56 years.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, 'Defining Noncompliance: NPT Safeguards Agreements'; IAEA Board of Governors GOV/2025/38

evidence.claim: NPT verification at scale in 2024: safeguards applied for 190 states, more than 3,000 in-field verification activities at more than 1,300 nuclear facilities and locations outside facilities, safeguards conclusions drawn for 175 of 190 states. The NPT was extended indefinitely on 1995-05-11; one party, the DPRK, has left, in 2003.
evidence.source: IAEA Safeguards Implementation Report for 2024

evidence.claim: CWC: opened 1993-01-13, in force 1997-04-29, 193 states parties. On 2023-07-07 the OPCW verified that the entire declared stockpile of 72,304 metric tonnes had been irreversibly destroyed. The Article IX challenge inspection has been invoked zero times in 29 years.
evidence.source: OPCW, 'All declared chemical weapons stockpiles verified as irreversibly destroyed'; OPCW Article IX

evidence.claim: Syria acceded to the CWC on 2013-10-14 and the OPCW Investigation and Identification Team subsequently attributed five chemical attacks to the Syrian Arab Air Force: Ltamenah on 24, 25 and 30 March 2017, Saraqib on 2018-02-04, Douma on 2018-04-07. Syria's rights and privileges under the convention were suspended on 2021-04-21.
evidence.source: OPCW, Investigation and Identification Team first, second and third reports

evidence.claim: BWC: opened 1972-04-10, in force 1975-03-26, 189 states parties, 51.4 years with zero verification provisions. Negotiation of a legally binding verification protocol ran through the Ad Hoc Group and collapsed in July 2001. The Soviet Union ran Biopreparat from 1974 with 30,000 to 40,000 staff across dozens of institutes while a party to the convention.
evidence.source: VERTIC Yearbook 2001, Chevrier, 'The Biological Weapons Convention: the protocol that almost was'; Kent Consortium for World Affairs, Biopreparat

evidence.claim: CTBT: opened for signature 1996-09-24 and 29.9 years later has not entered into force; Putin signed the deratification bill on 2023-11-02 after the Duma voted on 2023-10-18. The International Monitoring System was built regardless of entry into force.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, 'Russia Deratifies Nuclear Test Ban Treaty'

evidence.claim: Threshold Test Ban Treaty: signed 1974-07-03, entered into force 1990-12-11 once verification protocols were agreed — a 16.4-year gap between signature and a working verification regime. It remains in force at 35.7 years.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, US-Soviet/Russian nuclear arms control agreements at a glance

evidence.claim: COCOM operated from November 1949 to its dissolution on 1994-03-31, 44.4 years, and gave every member a veto over another member's export. Its successor, the Wassenaar Arrangement, was agreed 1995-12-18 with 28 founding states, held its resumed plenary 11–12 July 1996 with 33 members, and implemented control lists from 1996-11-01. Russia was welcomed as a participating state on 11–12 September 1995.
evidence.source: Wassenaar Arrangement, Genesis of the Wassenaar Arrangement; Arms Control Association, 'The Wassenaar Arrangement' (January 1997)

evidence.claim: Wassenaar now has 42 participating states and requires unanimity; adding a single technology to the control list can take up to three years. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine Russia has vetoed control-list updates, and the EU responded with a '500 series' of emerging-technology controls agreed outside the regime, alongside 11 separate national control actions by allied states between January and October 2024.
evidence.source: CSIS, 'Rethinking the Wassenaar Minus One Strategy'

evidence.claim: MTCR: founded 1987 by the G7, now 35 partners, voluntary and non-binding with no verification body. China committed in 1992 to abide by the guidelines and subsequently declined to adhere to the updated 1993 guidelines; it has transferred missile technology to Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Turkey and is alleged to have assisted Iran and North Korea.
evidence.source: SIPRI, 'The Missile Technology Control Regime at a crossroads'; NTI, MTCR

evidence.claim: NSG: formed 1975 after India's May 1974 test; the full-scope safeguards requirement was codified in the 1992 guidelines (INFCIRC/254 Part 1, paragraph 4); the 46 participating governments agreed an India-specific exemption from that requirement by consensus at an extraordinary plenary on 2008-09-06. The Australia Group first met in Brussels in June 1985 and has 43 members since India joined in 2018.
evidence.source: Arms Control Association, Nuclear Suppliers Group at a Glance; NTI, Australia Group

evidence.claim: Outside-view anchor: 1,547 denunciations and withdrawals were filed against multilateral treaties registered with the UN between 1945 and 2004, and only 3.5% of multilateral treaties experienced any withdrawal at all in that period. Security agreements between adversaries exit at roughly ten times that per-treaty rate.
evidence.source: Laurence R. Helfer, 'Exiting Treaties', Virginia Law Review 91:1579

evidence.claim: No instrument in this record pairs the United States with China in a binding limit on a technology. The nearest cases are the November 2024 Biden–Xi statement on human control of nuclear-use decisions, which China's November 2025 arms-control white paper restated around 'relevant weapons systems' in place of nuclear ones, and a bilateral AI governance channel announced after the 14–15 May 2026 Beijing summit.
evidence.source: IISS, 'Military AI governance under strain: the US–China dialogue'

evidence.claim: Verification for AI is at the stage the Threshold Test Ban Treaty was at in 1974. Baker's survey of three classes of nuclear verification argues the challenges reduce to levels already managed given privacy-preserving hardware inspection methods; Peigné, Nguyen and Wang estimate a deployable zero-knowledge training-verification proof of concept in approximately 36 months at single-digit-percent training-side overhead, against a six-to-ten-year timeline for custom verification silicon, with thirteen open research problems named.
evidence.source: Mauricio Baker, arXiv:2304.04123; Peigné, Nguyen and Wang, arXiv:2606.05433

recommendedNumber:
Three separate hazards, by regime type. I coded 21 instruments; the arithmetic is per agreement-year in force, to 2026-08-17.

TIER A — bilateral limits between the adversary pair (the direct analogue for a US–China AI deal). Nine instruments that entered force, with years in force:
SALT I 5.0 (1972-10-03 to 1977-10-03), ABM 29.7, TTBT 35.7 (running), INF 31.2, START I 15.0, SORT 7.7, New START 15.0, Agreed Framework 8.2, Incidents at Sea 54.2 (running). Sum = 201.6 agreement-years.
Endings with no replacement in force: ABM (withdrawal), INF (withdrawal), Agreed Framework (collapse), SALT I (expiry), New START (expiry) = 5.
LAPSE = 5 / 201.6 = 2.48% per year. Per decade: 1 − 0.9752^10 = 22.2%.
Poisson 90% interval on 5 events: λ ∈ [1.97, 10.51] → 0.98% to 5.21% per year → 9.4% to 41.5% per decade.
Restricting to unilateral exit before term: 3 / 201.6 = 1.49% per year → 14.0% per decade. Use this as the floor.

VIOLATION, Tier A. Four instruments carry a documented material breach: ABM (Krasnoyarsk, admitted 1989-10-23), INF (9M729), Agreed Framework (DPRK enrichment, 2002-10-16), New START (US determination 2023-01-31). Time at risk to first violation: ABM 10.3, INF 20.0, Agreed Framework 8.0, New START 11.9; the five clean instruments contribute their full 117.6 years. Total 167.8 agreement-years.
VIOLATION = 4 / 167.8 = 2.38% per year. Per decade: 1 − 0.97616^10 = 21.4%.
Poisson 90% interval on 4 events: λ ∈ [1.37, 9.15] → 0.81% to 5.45% per year → 7.8% to 42.5% per decade.
Cross-check: Lippert's 8 severe violations in 40 conventional agreements = 20% of agreements, against my 4/9 = 44% under a looser "any documented material breach" bar. The two bracket the truth; 20% to 44% lifetime, ~2.4% per year, is the defensible band.

TIER B — multilateral with a verification organ. NPT 56.5, CWC 29.3, BWC 51.4, PTBT 62.9, Open Skies 18.9, CFE 31.1 = 250.1 agreement-years. Collapses: Open Skies, CFE = 2.
LAPSE = 2 / 250.1 = 0.80% per year → 7.7% per decade. Violation touched 4 of 6 (NPT, CWC, BWC, CFE), so multilateralism plus verification buys durability at roughly one third the bilateral rate while leaving the violation rate where it was.

TIER C — informal export regimes, zero verification. COCOM 44.4, Zangger 55.0, NSG 51.0, Australia Group 41.2, MTCR 39.3, Wassenaar 29.8 = 260.7 regime-years, 1 dissolution (COCOM, 1994-03-31).
LAPSE = 1 / 260.7 = 0.38% per year → 3.8% per decade. The regime class that has never lapsed is the class that never verified anything, and it is the class that freezes when the adversary sits inside it: Wassenaar's 42 members need unanimity, one technology takes up to three years to list, and Russia has vetoed updates since 2022.

THE CONDITIONAL THE MODEL SHOULD CARRY. Of the four Tier A agreements that were violated, four ended. Lags from finding to termination: Agreed Framework 0.2 years, New START 3.0, INF 5.1, ABM 12.6; median 4.1 years. Of the five that were not violated, two are still in force and three expired at their scheduled term. So P(agreement ends | documented violation) = 4/4, on four events — treat as 0.8 to 0.9 with a wide band, not 1.0.

WHAT TO PUT IN THE MODEL. For a bilateral US–China agreement with on-site or technical verification, over a 10-year horizon:
  P(lapse) = 0.22, band 0.09 to 0.42
  P(violation by at least one party) = 0.21, band 0.08 to 0.43
  P(still in force and verified at 10 years) ≈ (1 − 0.22) × (1 − 0.21 × 0.85) = 0.78 × 0.822 = 0.64
If the agreement is instead a multilateral instrument with an inspectorate, multiply the lapse hazard by 0.80/2.48 = 0.32. If it is an informal export-control-style arrangement, multiply by 0.38/2.48 = 0.15 for lapse and treat compliance as unmeasured.

TWO ADJUSTMENTS THE RAW RATE MISSES.
1. Verification uptime. On-site inspection ran for 13.0 of INF's 31.2 years and 9.1 of New START's 15.0 — 22.1 of 46.2 years, 47.8%. The modal failure is a live text with dead verification under it, which the lapse rate scores as success. Apply a 0.5 multiplier to any "agreement in force" term that the model treats as implying monitoring.
2. Time to teeth. The TTBT took 16.4 years from signature (1974-07-03) to entry into force with agreed verification protocols (1990-12-11); the CWC took 4.3 years; the CTBT has taken 29.9 years and counting; the BWC never got there. Median across the cases that arrived: about 10 years. An AI agreement signed in year t should carry verification from roughly t+4 to t+16, with a real branch where it never arrives — and Peigné et al. put a zero-knowledge training proof of concept at approximately 36 months with thirteen open problems, so t+4 is the optimistic end.
whatWouldSettleIt:
Two measurements, neither of which exists in published form.

First, a coded dataset of WMD and dual-use agreements 1945–2026 on Lippert's schema. Lippert's 40 cases are conventional arms in Europe; the 21-instrument nuclear, chemical, biological and export-control table above is my own coding and has not been through review. The columns that matter and that nobody publishes: agreement-years in force, a 0–1 violation severity score, the identity of the adjudicator who made each non-compliance finding, and the outcome lag from finding to termination. My violation numerator rests on four events adjudicated four different ways — one self-admission (Krasnoyarsk, 1989-10-23), one DPRK admission (2002-10-16), and two US State Department determinations that Russia disputes (INF 2014, New START 2023-01-31). A dataset with a third-party adjudicator column would move the 2.38% per year figure by an amount I cannot currently bound.

Second, verification uptime as a published series: for each treaty, the fraction of its life during which its inspection regime actually operated. I computed 47.8% for INF and New START by hand from two secondary sources. If someone published that series across the 21 instruments, the lapse rate and the "in force" flag would stop being the same measurement, and the model could separate a treaty that is alive from one that is merely unrepealed.

The residual gap that no dataset closes: zero of the 21 instruments pair the United States with China in a binding limit on a technology, and the closest thing to a precedent — the November 2024 statement on human control of nuclear-use decisions — was restated in China's November 2025 white paper around 'relevant weapons systems' within twelve months. Every number above transfers to the US–China AI case by analogy to the US–Soviet case, and the analogy carries a bloc structure, a shared verification culture built over the 16.4 years between TTBT signature and entry into force, and an economic non-relationship, none of which hold now. State the numbers as a US–Soviet base rate and carry the transfer as an explicit assumption with its own uncertainty, rather than folding it into the band.

headline: Congress preempts state technology regulation at roughly 3 enactments per 19 Congress-opportunities (16% per Congress) and only when the preemption carries a federal replacement standard — a condition every AI vehicle failed until the June 4, 2026 Obernolte-Trahan draft, which as of August 2026 remains unintroduced, while the executive-only channel rests on a Colorado complaint pleading four constitutional counts and zero statutory-preemption counts.

evidence.claim: The Senate struck the 10-year state AI moratorium from the budget reconciliation bill 99-1 during a 27-hour vote-a-rama, on a Markey-Cantwell-Blackburn amendment; Thom Tillis (R-NC) cast the single no vote. This is the only recorded floor vote on AI preemption in either chamber.
evidence.source: U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce, Science & Transportation, press release

evidence.claim: State AI preemption language shopped by House Majority Leader Scalise was dropped from the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act; Scalise announced Congress would omit it. Second failed congressional attempt in six months, both under unified party control.
evidence.source: Americans for Responsible Innovation, 'AI Law Preemption Dropped from NDAA'; StateScoop

evidence.claim: Executive Order 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence' signed December 11, 2025 directed the Attorney General to establish an AI Litigation Task Force by January 10, 2026 to challenge state AI laws as burdens on interstate commerce or as preempted. The task force was established January 9, 2026 and had filed no complaint of its own as of late March 2026. The EO carves out three areas: child safety, AI compute and data-center infrastructure, and state procurement.
evidence.source: Paul Hastings client alert; BakerHostetler, 'Navigating the Emerging Federal-State AI Showdown'

evidence.claim: The White House released its National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence, asking Congress to enact statutory preemption of state AI laws deemed unduly burdensome while preserving state police powers over children, fraud and general consumer protection. It is a request to Congress, carrying no operative preemptive force of its own.
evidence.source: Ropes & Gray; Morgan Lewis; WilmerHale client alerts

evidence.claim: xAI v. Weiser, No. 1:26-cv-01515 (D. Colo.): complaint filed April 9, 2026; United States intervened as plaintiff April 24, 2026; court stayed enforcement of Colorado SB 24-205 and vacated all deadlines April 27, 2026. xAI asserts six claims under the First Amendment, Commerce Clause, Due Process Clause and Equal Protection Clause — four constitutional theories and zero federal statutory preemption counts, because no federal AI statute exists to preempt with. The most recent docket entry is April 27, 2026; the preliminary injunction motion is due 28 days after Colorado finalizes implementing rulemaking, so no merits ruling exists.
evidence.source: Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse docket, clearinghouse.net/case/48129; Norton Rose Fulbright

evidence.claim: The Supreme Court unanimously rejected the 'almost per se' rule against state laws with extraterritorial effects and upheld California Proposition 12 under Pike balancing. This removes the principal dormant Commerce Clause theory available against out-of-state-effect state AI laws.
evidence.source: National Pork Producers Council v. Ross, 598 U.S. 356 (2023), supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/21-468_5if6.pdf

evidence.claim: The D.C. Circuit upheld the bulk of the FCC's Restoring Internet Freedom Order and vacated its Preemption Directive, holding the Commission had shown no legal authority to bar states from imposing requirements more stringent than the federal order. The Ninth Circuit then upheld California's SB 822 in ACA Connects v. Bonta on January 28, 2022 — 3 years 4 months after the state law's September 30, 2018 enactment. Closest precedent for executive-branch preemption attempted without a congressional grant: the state law survived.
evidence.source: Mozilla Corp. v. FCC, 940 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2019); CRS LSB10693 on ACA Connects v. Bonta

evidence.claim: ACIR inventory of federal preemption statutes 1790-1991: 439 total, by decade — before 1900: 30; 1900s: 14; 1910s: 22; 1920s: 17; 1930s: 33; 1940s: 16; 1950s: 27; 1960s: 47; 1970s: 108; 1980s: 100; 1990-91: 25. Commerce accounts for 176 of 439 (40%). The modern rate is roughly 10-12 preemption statutes enacted per year across all subject areas.
evidence.source: U.S. Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations, 'Federal Statutory Preemption of State and Local Authority: History, Inventory, and Issues,' A-121, Table 1-1, p.9 (extracted from the primary PDF)

evidence.claim: Across 135 Supreme Court preemption decisions spanning the Rehnquist and Roberts Courts, 55% were decided in favor of preemption; the Roberts Court found preemption in 71% of its 28 cases, a difference significant at the 5% level. Preemption cases run about 7-8% of the civil docket, averaging 5 per term. Every case in this set involved a federal statute doing the preempting.
evidence.source: Greve, Klick, Petrino & Sevilla, 'Preemption in the Rehnquist and Roberts Courts: An Empirical Analysis,' 23 Supreme Court Economic Review 353, Tables 2-3 (extracted from the primary PDF)

evidence.claim: Case studies of congressional preemption of state technology regulation, with gaps from first state regulation to federal preemption: commercial aviation ~5 years (states early 1950s, Federal Aviation Act 1958); vehicle emissions ~5-7 years (California early 1960s, federal 1965-67); nutrition labeling ~2-3 years (states late 1980s, NLEA 1990); GM food labeling under 1 month from the state law taking effect. The stated finding: Congress does not preempt state law without enacting a federal replacement, and preemption succeeds as a compromise between a pro-regulatory camp and an industry coalition.
evidence.source: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 'When Should Congress Preempt State AI Law? The Lessons of Past Technologies'

evidence.claim: Vermont Act 120 passed May 2014 and took effect July 1, 2016; President Obama signed S.764 establishing the National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard on July 29, 2016; the Vermont AG ceased enforcement August 2, 2016. Gap: 2 years 3 months from state enactment, 4 weeks from state effective date. Fastest congressional preemption in the comparison set, and it carried a federal replacement standard.
evidence.source: National Agricultural Law Center; Office of the Vermont Attorney General; VTDigger

evidence.claim: California SB 186 was signed September 23, 2003 with a January 1, 2004 effective date; CAN-SPAM was signed December 16, 2003 and preempted the tougher state law before it took effect — a 3-month gap, 6 years after Nevada's first state anti-spam law in 1997. CAN-SPAM carried a federal substantive regime enforced by the FTC.
evidence.source: Dorsey & Whitney client publication; Stimmel Law; Mondaq

evidence.claim: The Internet Tax Freedom Act was enacted October 21, 1998 as a 3-year moratorium (October 1, 1998 to October 1, 2001) on new state taxes on internet access, grandfathering 9 states that already taxed access (HI, NH, NM, ND, OH, SD, TX, WA, WI). The only pure moratorium in the comparison set to pass: short duration, existing state laws preserved, and a subject where Commerce Clause authority is at its clearest.
evidence.source: CRS IF11947, 'The Internet Tax Freedom Act and Federal Preemption'; GAO-06-273

evidence.claim: Autonomous vehicles: Nevada AB 511 (June 2011) was the first state AV law. The SELF DRIVE Act passed the House in 2017; the AV START Act (S.1885) never reached the Senate floor and died with the 115th Congress. A third attempt was introduced February 2026, and House Transportation & Infrastructure advanced H.R. 8870 by 62-2 on May 22, 2026, covering commercial motor vehicles only, with no Senate action. 15 years and five Congresses of live preemption bills with zero enactments.
evidence.source: Eno Center for Transportation; Holland & Knight, 'House Passes Autonomous Vehicles Framework'; Upstream Security

evidence.claim: Comprehensive consumer privacy: the ADPPA cleared House Energy & Commerce 53-2 on July 20, 2022, with an amendment to strike preemption rejected 8-48, and never received a floor vote in either chamber. That remains the high-water mark for a preemptive federal tech statute. California's CCPA was signed June 28, 2018, so state privacy law has stood 8 years across five Congresses.
evidence.source: National Law Review; IAPP; The Hill; Wikipedia (ADPPA)

evidence.claim: Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act on June 4, 2026: 3-year preemption of state laws specifically regulating AI model development, states retaining authority over AI use, plus frontier transparency duties, critical safety incident reporting, whistleblower protections, and CAISI authorization at $100 million per year for FY2027-29. It is the first AI vehicle to pair preemption with a federal replacement standard. As of July 2026 it remains a discussion draft, drew opposition from House Democrats led by Ted Lieu and from Republicans wanting broader preemption, and was assessed as unlikely to pass in 2026 given remaining legislative days.
evidence.source: Covington Global Policy Watch, 'Backlash to Bipartisan AI Omnibus Illustrates Preemption Impasse'; Roll Call; TechPolicy.Press; Rep. Obernolte press release

evidence.claim: 84 new AI-related laws were enacted in 27 states in 2026 as of the July 21, 2026 mid-year report, following 145 in 2025, with seven states still in session (CA, MI, PA, MA, OH, NJ, NC). No federal statute or court has preempted or paused any state AI law as of June 2026 outside the single stayed Colorado statute.
evidence.source: Transparency Coalition AI Legislative Update, July 31, 2026; Cloud Security Alliance research note

recommendedNumber:
HAZARD RATE, CONSTRUCTED FROM DATED CASES (my assembly, no published study exists):
Count Congresses in which a federal preemption bill for a specific technology field was live, against enactments.
- Internet access taxes: 105th → enacted. 1/1
- Spam: 105th, 106th, 107th, 108th → enacted in 108th. 1/4
- GM food labeling: 113th, 114th → enacted in 114th. 1/2
- Autonomous vehicles: 115th, 116th, 117th, 118th, 119th → 0/5
- Comprehensive privacy: 115th, 116th, 117th, 118th, 119th → 0/5
- Net neutrality: 115th, 116th → 0/2
Total: 3 enactments / 19 Congress-opportunities = 15.8% per Congress ≈ 8% per year.

SPLIT BY THE CARNEGIE DISCRIMINATOR (does the bill carry a federal replacement standard?):
- With a replacement standard: aviation, vehicle emissions, nutrition labeling, GMO labeling, spam → 5 of 5 eventually enacted. Median gap from first state law ≈ 3 years (range: 4 weeks after Vermont's law took effect, to 7 years for emissions).
- Pure moratorium with no replacement: 1 of 3. ITFA passed (Oct 21, 1998) at 3 years' duration with 9 states grandfathered; the AI 10-year moratorium went down 99-1 (Jul 1, 2025) and was dropped from the NDAA (Dec 2025).

AI-SPECIFIC ADJUSTMENT: none upward for unified party control. Both AI failures occurred under unified control, so that factor sits inside the base rate already. The 99-1 vote is a recorded vote of the chamber that must pass this, and no other case in the set carries a comparable pre-enactment signal.

CONGRESSIONAL PATH:
- Remainder of 119th (Aug 17, 2026 → Jan 3, 2027, 4.5 months, midterms Nov 3, 2026, vehicle still a discussion draft): 0.158 × (4.5/24) ≈ 3%. Use 3-5%.
- 120th Congress (2027-28): hold 16%, +2pp because GAAIA is the first vehicle matching the 5-of-5 template, -2pp for the July 2026 two-flank opposition. Net 15-18%.
- P(preemption statute enacted by end 2028) = 1 - (1-0.04)(1-0.17) = 20%.

JUDICIAL PATH: the 55%/135-case and 71%/28-case SCOTUS rates are inapplicable — all those cases had a federal statute, and the DOJ's own Colorado complaint carries zero statutory-preemption counts. Governing precedents run against: Mozilla (Oct 1, 2019) vacated executive preemption for want of authority; NPPC v. Ross (May 11, 2023) killed the extraterritoriality theory. Timing from the net-neutrality analogue is 3 years 4 months state-enactment to circuit merits ruling, and xAI v. Weiser has no PI motion yet (stayed Apr 27, 2026 pending Colorado rulemaking), putting a circuit ruling in 2028 at the earliest. P(broad judicial invalidation by end 2028) ≈ 8-10%.

RECOMMENDED PRIORS:
- P(binding federal preemption of state AI law in force by Dec 31, 2027) = 1 - (1-0.10)(1-0.03) ≈ 12%. Band 8-15%.
- P(by Dec 31, 2028) = 1 - (1-0.20)(1-0.09) ≈ 27%. Band 20-30%, point 25%.
- Conditional worth carrying separately: P(enactment | a bill pairing preemption with a substantive federal standard reaches committee markup) ≈ 70-80%, from 5 of 5 in the historical set discounted for the two AI-specific failures. Markup is the observable that should move this axis, and it has not happened.
- Distinguish the events: P(specific provisions of specific state AI laws struck on First Amendment grounds by end 2028) is materially higher, ~50-60%, and produces no field preemption.
whatWouldSettleIt:
Four measurements, in order of how much each moves the number.

1. A committee markup of the Great American AI Act or any successor pairing preemption with a substantive federal standard. This single event shifts the estimate from the 3-in-19 branch (16% per Congress) to the 5-of-5 branch (70-80%). It is publicly observable on House Energy & Commerce's markup calendar and has not occurred as of August 17, 2026.

2. A second recorded floor vote on any AI preemption text. The model currently leans on one observation, July 1, 2025, 99-1. One vote is a thin reed for a probability this load-bearing, and the whip count on a narrowed 3-year development-only preemption is unmeasured.

3. The first merits ruling in xAI v. Weiser. The April 27, 2026 order starts a 28-day preliminary-injunction clock from Colorado's final adoption of implementing rulemaking, so tracking the Colorado rulemaking docket gives advance notice. A ruling on the dormant Commerce Clause count after National Pork Producers would be the first real read on whether the executive-only channel has any force; a ruling confined to the First Amendment counts would confirm the provision-by-provision path and leave the preemption axis where it is.

4. A published hazard-rate study. The 3-in-19 figure is my own assembly from dated cases, and the case set is one I chose — a different analyst picking different fields would get a different denominator. No peer-reviewed per-Congress hazard rate for technology preemption exists. A systematic count of every Congress since 1990 in which a field-specific preemption bill was reported out of committee, against enactments, would replace a constructed number with a measured one and would carry an honest confidence interval, which mine does not.

headline: The Gilens and Page near-zero result was overturned on 5 May 2026 by a demonstration that it is reproduced exactly from a data-generating process in which rich and poor have identical influence, and on the same 1,779 cases the general public's coefficient is 3.11 against business interests' 2.37; the technology-specific measurement of polling against enactment still does not exist, while state AI bills converted to law at 12.0% in 2025 and are tracking near 7.5% in 2026.

evidence.claim: The multivariate model that produced the near-zero result reports average citizens' preferences at .03 (SE .08), economic elites at .76 (.08), interest groups at .56 (.09), R-squared .074, on 1,779 policy cases from 1981-2002. The bivariate model for the same average-citizen series reports .64 (.08), p<.001. Preferences of average citizens and economic elites correlate at .78 after measurement-error correction.
evidence.source: Gilens & Page, 'Testing Theories of American Politics', Perspectives on Politics 12(3):564-581, Tables 2 and 3 (read from the Cambridge Core PDF)

evidence.claim: Gilens and Page's own descriptive figure: across their 1,779 cases, narrow pro-change majorities got the policy change they wanted about 30% of the time, and pro-change majorities of 80% of the public got the change about 43% of the time, within a four-year window.
evidence.source: Gilens & Page, Perspectives on Politics 12(3):564-581, section 'Majoritarian Electoral Democracy'

evidence.claim: Relative policy support of the 50th and 90th income percentiles correlates at r = 0.94 across the 1,836 survey questions in Gilens's data. Preference gaps of 10 points or less cover 82% of the observations; among the 18% with larger gaps the correlation is r = 0.68, and 66% of predicted values built from middle-income preferences fall inside the 95% confidence intervals of the affluent-based predictions, with none statistically different.
evidence.source: Enns, 'Relative Policy Support and Coincidental Representation', Perspectives on Politics 13(4):1053-1064 (read from the author's PDF)

evidence.claim: A ceiling on the whole system: in Gilens's data the expected probability of policy change almost never exceeds 0.5 even at the highest levels of public support, over a four-year window.
evidence.source: Enns, Perspectives on Politics 13(4):1053-1064

evidence.claim: Median-income Americans received their preferred outcome 47% of the time when the process had to choose between them and the wealthy, 1980-2002; high-income and median-income policy preferences correlate at 0.91; the Gilens and Page model accounts for about 7% of the variation in policy outcomes.
evidence.source: Bashir, 'Testing Inferences about American Politics', Research & Politics 2(4), and Bashir's own published summary of the paper

evidence.claim: Where middle-income and high-income preferences oppose each other, the rich prevail 53% of the time against the middle class's 47%; middle, rich and poor agree on the large majority of policies.
evidence.source: Branham, Soroka & Wlezien, 'When Do the Rich Win?', Political Science Quarterly 132(1):43-62 (read from the journal's published article summary; full text paywalled)

One regression, now runnable for the first time, and one publication.

headline: Six published decompositions exist and are enumerated below; Epoch's "60–95%" is the minimum and maximum across 12 overlapping model pairs in a single 2024 paper, it rises monotonically with how recent the baseline model is (72.2% at a 2012 baseline, 91.6% at a 2018 one), and the quantity the forecast actually needs — the physical share of effective-compute growth — computes to 50% with a 30–70% band, which puts the register's 60/40 at the top of the defensible range.

evidence.claim: The source of the 60–95% figure, stated verbatim in section 4.1: "A Shapley value-based analysis suggests that 60-95% of the performance gains stem from compute scaling, while algorithms contribute only 5-40%." Dataset is 200+ language model evaluations on WikiText and Penn Treebank, 2012–2023, pre-training only. Shapley computed in linear perplexity space over four factors: parameter scaling, data scaling, parameter efficiency, data efficiency. "Compute scaling" is parameter scaling plus data scaling, so data sits inside the 60–95%, not beside it.
evidence.source: Anson Ho, Tamay Besiroglu, Ege Erdil, David Owen, Robi Rahman, Zifan Carl Guo, David Atkinson, Neil Thompson, Jaime Sevilla, "Algorithmic progress in language models", arXiv:2403.05812 (Epoch AI / MIT FutureTech), NeurIPS 2024

evidence.claim: The 60–95% is a spread across model pairs, not an uncertainty interval, and it is monotone in baseline recency. Summing the parameter-scaling and data-scaling columns of Table 1 for each of the 12 rows gives: pairs based at the 2012 RNN average 72.2% (59.2, 67.1, 75.4, 81.0, 78.2); pairs based at the 2016 LSTM average 85.3% (79.3, 87.0, 89.3, 85.5); pairs based at the 2018 Transformer average 91.6% (95.0, 92.7, 87.2). The 95% endpoint is Transformer(2018) to GPT-2(2019), a one-year span across which little algorithmic progress could accrue by construction; the 59.2% endpoint is RNN(2012) to LSTM(2016). Twelve rows are built from five endpoints, so the rows are not independent draws.
evidence.source: Table 1, Ho et al., arXiv:2403.05812; row sums computed directly from the published table

evidence.claim: The computer-vision Shapley decomposition, on ~100 ImageNet models, splits progress differently: algorithms 24.9–70.6%, compute scaling 29.3–49.8%, data scaling 11.9–28.1%. Compute-plus-data across the three long spans that actually scaled data (AlexNet to BiT-L, ViT-H/14, ViT-e) is 59.3%, 56.3% and 58.4% — averaging 58.0%. The same baseline-recency gradient appears: AlexNet-based pairs average 47.7% compute-plus-data, ResNet50-based 66.7%, ResNeXt-101-based 71.6%. Robust to redoing the Shapley in log-odds space (Appendix F). Compute-augmenting algorithmic advances halve compute requirements every 9 months (95% CI 4 to 25 months).
evidence.source: Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu, "Algorithmic progress in computer vision", arXiv:2212.05153, Tables 2 and 3 (v4 2023-08-24)

evidence.claim: Epoch's own plain-language summary of the computer-vision result is close to an even split, not 60–95%: "Roughly, progress in image classification has been ~45% due to the scaling of compute, ~45% due to better algorithms, ~10% due to scaling data."
evidence.source: Epoch AI, "Revisiting algorithmic progress", epoch.ai/blog/revisiting-algorithmic-progress

evidence.claim: The first experimental decomposition, by ablation and scaling runs rather than observation. Two scale-dependent innovations — LSTM to Kaplan Transformer (846x) and Chinchilla rebalancing (~10x) — account for 91% of total measured efficiency gains extrapolated to the 2025 frontier of 2e23 FLOP. Every scale-invariant innovation they tested contributes under 10x combined, under 10% of the total. Their measured compute-equivalent-gain growth is 2.23x per year for a total of 6,930x over 2012–2023, against the 22,000x implied by Ho et al. 2024, leaving an unexplained gap of 3.18x.
evidence.source: Hans Gundlach, Alex Fogelson, Jayson Lynch, Ana Trišović, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Anmol Sandhu, Neil Thompson, "On the Origin of Algorithmic Progress in AI", arXiv:2511.21622 (MIT FutureTech)

evidence.claim: The same paper shows the whole quantity is ill-posed without naming a reference algorithm and a target compute scale: measuring a sequence of modern mixture-of-experts Transformers against an LSTM reference yields 63% annual growth in compute-equivalent gain, while measuring the same sequence against a dense Transformer reference yields a constant 2x multiplier and therefore 0% growth. Their words: "one can continue to measure arbitrarily large rates of progress from some fixed point while realizing none of these gains in practice."
evidence.source: Section 5.2 and Figure 7, Gundlach et al., arXiv:2511.21622

evidence.claim: An econometric objection to every observational estimate in this literature, including the one the register cites. If algorithmic quality is partly latent and compute choices are endogenous to it, the Ho et al. estimator is biased. Concretely: Hoffmann et al. 2022 and Besiroglu et al. 2024 estimate the data-scaling exponent beta experimentally at ~0.37, while Ho et al. 2024 estimate it at ~0.04; since the data-efficiency progress rate is recovered as beta_year divided by beta, "a first-pass estimate is that algorithmic progress is overstated by around a factor of nine." Monte Carlo on the actual Ho et al. dataset: at correlation 0.5 a true 45% annual progress rate is estimated as 16.5%; at correlation -0.5 it appears as 93%.
evidence.source: Parker Whitfill, "Note on Selection Bias in Observational Estimates of Algorithmic Progress", arXiv:2508.11033 (v2 2025-08-18)

evidence.claim: An independent cross-sectional decomposition on 809 models released 2022–2025, using scaling-law regressions with release-date and developer fixed effects: "At the frontier, 80–90% of performance differences are explained by higher training compute, implying that scale—not proprietary technology—drives frontier advances." This is variance explained among contemporaneous models, a different estimand from time-series attribution, and it is the only published figure that independently lands inside the upper half of Epoch's band. Away from the frontier the same firms show up to 40x compute-efficiency differences between two of their own models.
evidence.source: Matthias Mertens, Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni, Neil Thompson, "Is there 'Secret Sauce' in Large Language Model Development?", arXiv:2602.07238 (MIT), v2 2026-05-03

evidence.claim: The physical-compute rate the split depends on: training compute for notable models grew 4.1x per year (90% CI 3.7x to 4.6x) from 2010 to May 2024, and frontier language models have grown at 5x per year since 2020.
evidence.source: Epoch AI, "Training compute of frontier AI models grows by 4-5x per year"

evidence.claim: The authoritative synthesis position, and it is wider than the register assumes: "Algorithmic efficiency improvements have historically provided an additional 2–6x performance gain per year", with a central 3x, and the report classes this as an evidence gap — estimates "are unable to rule out rates ranging from 2–6x per year."
evidence.source: International AI Safety Report 2026, arXiv:2602.21012, capability and evidence-gap sections

evidence.claim: Once post-training is counted the algorithmic rate roughly triples, which inverts the split. Epoch's own current position: "after accounting for all training compute (including post-training), I think we're seeing software progress at around 10x per year, and my 80% credible interval would probably range from 2x to 50x per year." The same piece places Ho et al. 2024 at 3x/yr (pre-training only) and Gundlach et al. 2025 at 2.23x/yr.
evidence.source: Anson Ho, Epoch AI Gradient Updates, "The least understood driver of AI progress"

evidence.claim: An independent high-side estimate on the recent window: catch-up algorithmic progress including post-training over 2023–2025 runs "something like 16x–60x each year" (weighted analysis 1.76 orders of magnitude per year ≈ 60x, a 2-month halving; median analysis 16x, a 2.9-month halving), with a forward expectation of "maybe 20x with an 80% confidence interval of [2x–200x]".
evidence.source: Aaron Scher, MIRI Technical Governance Team, "Catch-Up Algorithmic Progress Might Actually be 60x per Year"

evidence.claim: The mechanism behind the post-training jump, measured: reasoning models trained with RL delivered a compute-equivalent gain "between 1x and 100x, with a central estimate of around 10x" on GPQA diamond, MATH Level 5 and Mock AIME, for GPT-4o to o1 and for Claude 3.5 to 3.7 Sonnet. Roughly 10x more pre-training compute would be needed to match the same performance without RL training.
evidence.source: Arden Berg and Anson Ho, Epoch AI Gradient Updates, "Quantifying the algorithmic improvement from reasoning models"

evidence.claim: The earliest measurement in the lineage, a pure efficiency series with no decomposition: the training FLOP needed to reach AlexNet-level ImageNet performance fell 44x between 2012 and 2019, a 16-month doubling, against 11x from hardware efficiency over the same period.
evidence.source: Danny Hernandez and Tom B. Brown, "Measuring the Algorithmic Efficiency of Neural Networks", arXiv:2005.04305 (OpenAI)

THE ESTIMAND THE MODEL NEEDS IS NOT THE ONE EPOCH REPORTS. `round-3-edges.md` uses the split to decide how much of effective-compute growth survives when physical compute is capped under S3. That is ln(g_physical) / ln(g_physical × g_algorithmic) — a share of a log growth rate. Epoch's 60–95% is a Shapley share of a perplexity reduction between two named models in linear space. The two coincide only when algorithmic progress is purely compute-augmenting, which both Epoch papers find it mostly is, so the log-rate route is the defensible one and the Shapley band should be dropped from the sizing.

PRE-TRAINING READING. Physical 4.1x/yr (Epoch, 2010–May 2024, 90% CI 3.7–4.6x); algorithmic 3x/yr (Ho et al. 2024; IASR 2026 central). ln(4.1) = 1.411, ln(3) = 1.099, sum 2.510. Physical share = 1.411 / 2.510 = 56%, algorithmic 44%. Sweeping the IASR 2026 range: at 2x/yr, 1.411 / (1.411 + 0.693) = 67%; at 6x/yr, 1.411 / (1.411 + 1.792) = 44%. Band 44–67%, central 56%.

ALL-SOFTWARE READING, which the forecast window requires because RL post-training is live from 2024. Physical 4.5x/yr; algorithmic 10x/yr (Ho, Epoch, 2026-02-25, 80% CI 2–50x). ln(4.5) = 1.504, ln(10) = 2.303, sum 3.807. Physical share = 1.504 / 3.807 = 40%, algorithmic 60%. Sweeping: at 2x/yr, 68%; at 50x/yr, 1.504 / (1.504 + 3.912) = 28%. Band 28–68%.

CROSS-CHECK. Gundlach et al. characterise the record as ~7 orders of magnitude of compute scaling against >4 of algorithmic gain: 7 / (7 + 4) = 64%. Using their own measured 6,930x (3.84 OOM): 7 / 10.84 = 65%.

RECOMMENDED SPLIT: 50% physical / 50% algorithmic, band 30–70%. The register's 60/40 sits at the top of that band. Move it down 10 points, or keep 60/40 and label it explicitly as the pre-training-only reading.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE S3 EDGE. Retardation factor = ln(g_physical,capped × g_algo) / ln(g_physical,baseline × g_algo), physical capped at 1.5x/yr against a 4.5x/yr baseline, as the register already assumes.

  algo 3x/yr:  ln(4.5) / ln(13.5) = 1.504 / 2.603 = 0.578   ← the register's 0.605, near enough
  algo 10x/yr: ln(15) / ln(45)  = 2.708 / 3.807 = 0.711

METR's 212-day doubling stretches to 212 / 0.65 = 326 days, band 279–424, against the register's 350. The one-month-horizon date moves from 2030–31 out to roughly 2032–34, about a year nearer than the register's 2033–35. The S3 multipliers on T soften accordingly, from ×0.45 / ×0.70 / ×1.20 / ×1.55 toward roughly ×0.52 / ×0.76 / ×1.17 / ×1.45. The direction is that a compute-supply constraint bites less than the register currently has it, because the algorithmic term that keeps running is larger than 40% once post-training counts.

DO NOT USE 60–95% AS A BAND. It is the minimum and maximum of 12 overlapping rows built from 5 endpoints, and it is monotone in baseline recency: 72.2% at a 2012 baseline, 85.3% at 2016, 91.6% at 2018. Taking its midpoint of 77.5% would import a short-span artifact — the 95% row spans one year, 2018 to 2019 — and would push the physical share ~20 points above every rate-based route.
whatWouldSettleIt:
A 2x2 at frontier scale: train the 2019 recipe and the 2025 recipe each at 1e23 and at 1e25 FLOP, and report the compute-equivalent gain at both scales. That single design settles all three live objections at once. It identifies the algorithm-by-scale interaction that Gundlach et al. showed is 91% of the effect and that observational Shapley estimates absorb into a calendar-year coefficient. It answers Whitfill's endogeneity objection, because compute is assigned rather than chosen by a lab that already knows its own algorithmic quality. And it forces the reference algorithm and the target compute scale to be named, without which Gundlach et al. show the growth rate can be reported as anything between 0% and 63% per year for the identical sequence of models. Gundlach et al. ran exactly this design in November 2025 and it is why theirs is the strongest evidence in the set — but at 3.6M parameters and 1.6M–29M-parameter scaling runs, five to eight orders of magnitude below the frontier they extrapolate to, which is the whole distance the finding is about.

Second best, and far cheaper: any frontier lab publishing training compute and benchmark score for a fixed-recipe control run repeated annually — the same architecture, data mix and hyperparameters, retrained each year at that year's compute. The gap between the control and the year's production model is the algorithmic term, measured rather than inferred. No lab publishes this. Anthropic's RSP carries an informal ~3x/yr figure with no run behind it.

Failing either, the falsifiable near-term test: Epoch's ~10x/yr all-software figure (2026-02-25) and Scher's 16–60x/yr (2025-12-24) imply that by 2028 a model matching April 2026 frontier capability should be trainable for 100x to 3,600x less total compute than it took in April 2026. Gundlach's 2.23x/yr implies about 5x. Those diverge by two to three orders of magnitude inside two years, and the Epoch Capabilities Index published 2025-11-28 is already the instrument that would read the answer off a compute-versus-ECI frontier. Watch that frontier through 2027–28; it separates the readings without anyone running a new experiment.
